 Indian state scraps Friday weekly holiday for Islamic schools
 Decision part of wider restructuring of minority education in Uttarakhand, officials say
 Bijay Kumar Minj 
 Updated: October 23, 2026 10:51 AM GMT 
 A file image showing boys studying the Koran at a madrasa or Islamic school in Guwahati, in India's northeastern state of Assam. (Photo: AFP)
 Indian minority rights activists have criticized a provincial government's decision to abolish the traditional Friday weekly holiday (Jumu'ah) in recognized madrasas, or schools imparting Islamic religious teachings, in the northern state of Uttarakhand.
 The Oct. 21 decision by the state education department has replaced Friday with a Sunday weekly off. Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami of the pro-Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) defended the decision, saying it was intended to bring uniformity to the state's education system.
 There should be a consistent system for everyone, and all educational institutions should move in the same direction, Dhami was quoted as saying by the Hindustan Times newspaper.
 Officials said the decision is part of the wider restructuring of minority education in Uttarakhand, where the government has replaced the state's Madrasa Education Board with the Uttarakhand State Authority for Minority Education on July 1.
 The new authority regulates educational institutions run by all notified minority communities, including Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains and Parsis.
 Officials said 76 madrasas had received recognition from the education department, while another 114 applications were being processed.
 The state previously had 452 madrasas registered under the now-abolished board. More than 200 were sealed in a crackdown on unrecognized madrasas in March 2025
 Surjeet Singh Gandhi, chairman of the new authority, said those institutions recognized as schools must comply with new regulations, including the prescribed weekly holiday, failing which they could face action.
 Community leaders have been consulted about the Friday prayer timings, and the school schedule would allow Muslim students and staff to attend the afternoon prayers, he added.
 Muhammad Arif, convenor of the All India Secular Forum, described the move as an attack on the constitutional rights of minority communities and accused the BJP government of pursuing a divisive agenda.
 First, the state government implemented the Uniform Civil Code, and now it is trying to control the educational institutions of minority communities, he told UCA News on Oct. 23.
 Arif said minority institutions have traditionally enjoyed the right to administer their educational establishments according to their own traditions, rules and regulations.
 Under the new arrangement, they will have very little say, while the government may attempt to impose its own agenda, he added.
 A.C. Michael, founder and national coordinator of the ecumenical United Christian Forum, said the decision did not surprise him, given what he described as a broader pattern of pressure on religious minorities. 
 He said the Uttarakhand government's decision reinforced his concerns about the position of religious minorities in India, where the idea of a Hindu nation had gained ground.
 Minority communities could face further restrictions if the government continued to introduce such policies, he added.
 Pratima Singh, a spokesperson for the opposition Congress party, accused the BJP government of politicizing education ahead of the state assembly elections expected in 2027.
 She questioned why the government was focusing on madrasas and Muslim religious practices instead of addressing broader challenges facing the education system.
